steps.body: Products often pass one whole. One whole holds exactly b of its own b-pieces, so any product with more than b pieces is greater than one.
steps.narration: Products often pass one whole. One whole holds exactly b of its own b-pieces, so any product with more than b pieces is greater than one.

widget.prompt: Build 3 × 3/4 and compare it to one whole.
widget.successFeedback: 9/4 — nine fourths, and since a whole holds four, this is more than two wholes.
widget.lowFeedback: Your bar represents less than the target value. Increase it until the values match.
widget.highFeedback: Your bar represents more than the target value. Decrease it until the values match.

commonFractions.feedback: 3/4 is one group, still under a whole.
4/4 is exactly one whole; nine fourths passes it more than twice.

predict.prompt: Is 5 × 3/4 more or less than one whole?
predict.reveal: Five groups of nearly-a-whole cannot stay under one; fifteen fourths is almost four wholes.

cml.actionGoal: Collect equal groups of a fraction and watch only the COUNT of pieces change for g4x past one.
invariants: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number collects groups of identical pieces: the denominator names the piece size and holds still, while the numerator counts every piece gathered, which is what keeps g4x past one a counting problem.
misconceptions: Scaling the denominator along with the numerator, adding the whole number to the numerator, or assuming a product cannot pass one whole.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the denominator DID change when you collected groups, what would happen to the size of each piece?

widget.prompt: Why is 5 × 3/4 greater than one whole?

options.label: Because 15 fourths is far more than the 4 fourths in one whole
options.feedback: Correct — one whole holds only 4 fourths, and this product collects 15 of them.

options.label: Because a product is always bigger than its factors
options.feedback: Not always — multiplying by a fraction less than one makes things smaller. Here the WHOLE-number factor is what grows it.

options.label: Because 3/4 is greater than one
options.feedback: 3/4 is less than one whole; it is taking five of them that passes one.

options.label: It is not — fractions are always less than one
options.feedback: Improper fractions like 15/4 are genuinely greater than one; fractions are not capped at a whole.

widget.prompt: Retrieve in a new form: Order 7/8, 2/8, and 5/8 from least to greatest. Which one is in the MIDDLE?

options.feedback: Correct — the pieces are identical eighths, so ordering the counts orders the fractions, and 5 sits between 2 and 7.
7/8 holds the MOST of these identical pieces, so it is the greatest, not the middle.
2/8 holds the FEWEST of these identical pieces, so it is the least, not the middle.
